what_changed: Telegram sticker egress extended from static (.png/.webp) and raster video (.webm) to animated vector (.tgs, gzipped Lottie), and from a single rigid silhouette to a rig whose parts animate independently.

measured.tgs_vs_webm_bytes: 16100 vs 228758 for the same motion — a 14x reduction
measured.reference_benchmark: a public 24-sticker animated reaction set the operator rates: 35-65 KB per sticker, 21-26 layers each with its own position/rotation/scale curves. Rigged parts, not one shape.
measured.our_rig: 2 layers (body, eyes) — the articulation gap is layer COUNT, not size

contract_findings: emoji parameter is `emojis`; the modern `emoji_list` name is refused with 'invalid sticker emojis' in every encoding tried (bare, repeated field, JSON array)
an animated sticker must be a direct multipart upload — a file_id from sendSticker is refused: 'animated sticker must be uploaded as an InputFile'
a .tgs must declare fr=60 and the top-level `tgs` marker; a lower frame rate returns 'wrong file type'
the emoji must be in Telegram's restricted sticker list; a non-member fails the call and silently omits one sticker from the set
verification: Every set above was read back with getStickerSet after publish and compared against its local manifest. A push returning ok is not the same claim as a set that contains the sticker: one sticker was silently absent from a live set while the push reported success.
limits: No additional photographs of the operator's cats exist on this machine: a sweep of 1687 unique images across the Photos Library originals and the Telegram media cache found none beyond 9 already known.
The rig is a first cut: 2 layers against the 21-26 of the reference set; further articulation (mouth, ears, tail) is the next step.
